title: 1958 Tybee Island mid-air collision
summary: During a night practice exercise, an F-86 fighter collided with a B-47 bomber at 38000 ft. The F-86 pilot ejected safely. The B-47 pilot regained control at 20000 ft and requested permission to jettison the 7600 lb Mark 15 nuclear bomb to reduce weight. title: Munich air disaster
summary: British European Airways Flight 609, an Airspeed Ambassador en route from Belgrade to Manchester, stopped at Munich to refuel. After two aborted takeoff attempts due to engine boost surging, the crew attempted a third takeoff in snow and slush. The aircraft failed to become airborne, struck a fence at runway end, and the left wing was torn off when it struck a house beyond the runway. Altogether 23 died and 21 survived.

title: Winter Hill air disaster
summary: A Bristol 170 Freighter chartered by Manx Airlines carrying motor trade personnel from the Isle of Man to Manchester was cleared to maintain 1500 feet altitude due to traffic and poor weather. While the captain was briefly absent from the cockpit, the first officer erroneously tuned the radio compass to Oldham Beacon instead of the correct Wigan Beacon. Visibility was extremely poor and Manchester Control ordered an immediate right turn but the aircraft crashed near the summit of Winter Hill in heavy snow. Thirty-five of the 42 aboard were killed.
probable_cause: First officer's error tuning the radio compass to the wrong beacon; captain's failure to confirm the correct tuning. Inquiry also ascribed blame to air traffic controllers and the aircraft's cockpit design with difficult-to-see navigation displays.

title: United Airlines 736

location.name: Southwest of Las Vegas, Clark County, Nevada

summary: United Air Lines Flight 736, a Douglas DC-7 with 47 passengers and crew aboard, was flying at 21,000 feet over Clark County, Nevada, on April 21, 1958, when it collided in midair with a United States Air Force F-100F Super Sabre fighter jet crewed by two pilots. Both aircraft fell out of control and crashed into unpopulated desert terrain southwest of Las Vegas, leaving no survivors. The collision occurred in clear weather at high altitude with high closure speeds. The investigation determined that structural supports on both aircraft's canopies limited pilot visibility and contributed to the inability to see the other aircraft until too late.
probable_cause: The high rate of near head-on closure and cockpit visibility limitations. A metal frame support on the F-100's canopy interfered with the Air Force instructor pilot's ability to see the oncoming DC-7, while a supporting pillar on the DC-7's windshield could have prevented the United Airlines captain from sighting the fighter until too late.

factors.evidence: The DC-7 airliner collided with the F-100F Super Sabre fighter jet at 21,000 feet.
ATC authorities at CAA and Nellis Air Force Base failed to reduce known collision risks and failed to coordinate traffic separation for training exercises.
A metal frame support on the F-100's canopy interfered with the Air Force instructor pilot's ability to see the oncoming DC-7.
The report faulted military and civilian aviation authorities for not reducing well-known collision risks that had existed for over a year.

title: Capital Airlines 300
summary: On 20 May 1958, a Vickers Viscount operated by Capital Airlines Flight 300 collided mid-air with a US Air Force Lockheed T-33 jet trainer in the airspace near Brunswick, Maryland. The Viscount had departed Pittsburgh for Baltimore at 10:50 local time and was descending through 8000 to 9000 feet when the T-33, traveling at significantly higher speed (290 knots versus 235 knots), banked right and impacted the left side of the Viscount forward of the wing. title: KLM 607-E
summary: KLM Flight 607-E, a Lockheed Super Constellation named Hugo de Groot on the second leg of a transatlantic trip from Amsterdam to New York, crashed into the Atlantic Ocean after departing Shannon Airport, Ireland, on 14 August 1958. Radio contact was lost about 35 minutes after takeoff, and a rescue operation later found light debris and recovered the remains of 34 of the 99 people aboard roughly 180 km northwest of Shannon. Irish and Dutch investigators could not pinpoint a definitive cause but believed the most likely explanation was an over-speeding outboard propeller, caused by metal particles obstructing an oil feed line regulator valve, which may have provoked a flight disturbance and caused the propeller to shear off.

title: Aeroflot 4
summary: The Tu-104A departed Khabarovsk and climbed to avoid towering cumulus clouds, reaching 12,000 m despite this being unsafe at the aircraft's takeoff weight of 66 tons. The aircraft encountered intense cumulonimbus clouds with strong updrafts that caused the aircraft to stall. Both engines flamed out during the stall, and the artificial horizons failed, rendering recovery nearly impossible.
probable_cause: The aircraft was flown to an unsafe altitude given its weight and encountered severe updrafts in cumulonimbus clouds, resulting in an aerodynamic stall. Insufficient analysis of weather conditions and lack of stall recovery procedures contributed to the accident.

factors.evidence: The aircraft climbed to 12000 m while weighted at 66 tons; altitudes of 12000 m could only be safely achieved in calm weather, and the weight limited maximum safe altitude to 11700 m at standard engine power.
Cumulonimbus clouds reaching altitudes of over 12000 m with strong updrafts between 11000 and the reported presence of strong updrafts within cumulonimbus clouds.
There were no defined procedures in place in the event of a stall, indicating lack of crew training for this situation.
The Tu-104 was prone to losing longitudinal stability in certain atmospheric conditions, could be followed by engine failure and artificial horizon failure.
The aircraft stalled, during which the engines flamed out and the landing gear was extended.
The aircraft crashed into a dense forest 215 km northwest of Khabarovsk airport, impacting the ground at an angle of 60°.

title: 1958 BOAC Bristol Britannia crash
summary: The Bristol Britannia was conducting a test flight on Christmas Eve 1958 when the crew requested clearance to descend from 12,000 feet to 3,000 feet for approach to Hurn Airport in thick fog. The crew misread the three-pointer altimeter believing they were at 11,500 feet when in fact at only 1,500 feet, causing them to fly the aircraft into fog-obscured terrain near Christchurch, killing 9 of the 12 persons on board.
probable_cause: Failure of the captain and first officer to correctly establish the aircraft's altitude before and during descent. The Britannia aircraft was fitted with a three-handed altimeter which required higher concentration to read correctly than desirable. Misreading of this instrument by the crew directly caused controlled flight into terrain in fog obscuring the ground.

events.text: Aircraft departed London Heathrow Airport for test flight to renew certificate of airworthiness with 12 persons including 5 crew
Crew requested clearance to descend from 12,000 feet to 3,000 feet for approach to Hurn Airport due to poor weather at Heathrow
Crew began descent but misread altimeter, believing altitude was 11,500 feet when actually at 1,500 feet
Aircraft struck ground in ploughed field near Christchurch crossing road, bringing down telephone lines and trees; all 12 on board killed or fatally injured
